blocks.text: A group of trekkers flies to a mountain town at 3,500 m and starts walking the same afternoon. By night one trekker has a throbbing headache, nausea and a broken night of sleep, while a colleague who ascended over several days feels fine. The air they breathed was still 21 percent oxygen, yet the physiology of the two climbers diverged. The explanation lies in pressure, not in the oxygen fraction.

blocks.markdown:
The composition of dry air does not change with height: the fractional concentration of oxygen (FiO2) is 0.21 from sea level to the summit of Everest. What changes is **barometric pressure (PB)**, which falls roughly exponentially with altitude because there is less atmosphere above you. Gas partial pressure is the fraction multiplied by total pressure (Dalton's law), so every gas partial pressure falls in proportion to PB. Oxygen moves down a pressure gradient, from air to alveolus to blood to mitochondria, so a lower partial pressure of oxygen at the start of this cascade means lower oxygen delivery at the end.

One more step matters. When air is inspired it is warmed to 37 degrees C and fully humidified in the airways, and water vapour exerts a partial pressure of 47 mmHg (PH2O) that does not depend on altitude. This is subtracted from PB before the oxygen fraction is applied.

blocks.title: Inspired and alveolar oxygen partial pressure
blocks.text: PIO2 is the partial pressure of oxygen in humidified inspired gas at the level of the trachea. PAO2 is the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveolar gas, which is lower than PIO2 because oxygen is continually removed into the blood and replaced by CO2 delivered from it. The respiratory exchange ratio R is the CO2 produced divided by the O2 consumed, taken as 0.8 at rest on a mixed diet. Hypoxaemia means low oxygen in arterial blood.

blocks.caption: Inspired oxygen partial pressure. FIO2 = 0.21; PB = barometric pressure (mmHg); PH2O = 47 mmHg at 37 degrees C.
Simplified alveolar gas equation. PACO2 is taken as equal to arterial PCO2 (mmHg); R = 0.8.

blocks.title: Inspired oxygen at sea level and at altitude
blocks.prompt: At sea level PB is 760 mmHg. At a high camp PB is 380 mmHg, about half. Calculate PIO2 at each and compare.

steps.text: Sea level: subtract water vapour, 760 - 47 = 713 mmHg of dry gas pressure.
Apply the oxygen fraction: 0.21 x 713 = 150 mmHg.
High camp: 380 - 47 = 333 mmHg, then 0.21 x 333 = 70 mmHg.
Compare: 70 / 150 = 0.47. PIO2 has fallen by more than half, because the fixed 47 mmHg water vapour takes a larger share of the smaller total pressure, even though FIO2 is unchanged.

blocks.answer: PIO2 is about 150 mmHg at sea level and about 70 mmHg at the high camp: oxygen fraction constant, partial pressure roughly halved.

blocks.title: How hyperventilation protects alveolar oxygen
blocks.prompt: At about 3,000 m, PIO2 is about 100 mmHg. A newly arrived climber has PACO2 of 40 mmHg. After hyperventilating, PACO2 is 30 mmHg. Calculate PAO2 in each case with R = 0.8.

steps.text: PAO2 = 100 - 37.5 = 62.5 mmHg, a gain of 12.5 mmHg for lowering PACO2 by only 10 mmHg.

blocks.answer: PAO2 rises from 50 to 62.5 mmHg: blowing off CO2 lets more oxygen occupy the alveolar gas.

blocks.markdown:
**Immediate ventilatory response.** The fall in arterial PO2 is detected by the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies (the glomus cells), which signal via the glossopharyngeal nerve to the medullary respiratory centres. Ventilation increases within minutes. But this hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and so raises arterial and cerebrospinal fluid pH. The central chemoreceptors, which respond to H+ in the brain extracellular fluid, now see an alkaline signal and oppose the increase. Ventilation therefore rises only modestly at first.

**Ventilatory acclimatisation over days.** The kidneys excrete bicarbonate, and bicarbonate also falls in cerebrospinal fluid. Plasma and CSF pH drift back towards normal, the brake from the central chemoreceptors is released, and ventilation rises further over several days. In addition, carotid body sensitivity to hypoxia increases. The result is a progressively lower PaCO2 and a higher PaO2 than on day one.

**Haematological response.** Hypoxia stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor in the peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney, which release erythropoietin. Erythropoietin stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow. Plasma volume also falls in the first days, which raises haemoglobin concentration quickly but without a real rise in red cell mass. New red cells take weeks, raising oxygen-carrying capacity.

blocks.caption: Timeline of adaptation to a sustained reduction in inspired oxygen.
rows: Carotid body detects low PaO2; increases ventilation
Alkaline CSF and plasma suppress central chemoreceptor drive
Falling bicarbonate restores pH; central brake released; more hypoxic sensitivity
Further rise in ventilation and PaO2
Erythropoietin from kidney stimulates marrow; early plasma volume fall

items: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) follows rapid ascent, typically above about 2,500 m, and presents with headache plus one or more of nausea, fatigue, dizziness and poor sleep.
Hypoxia causes cerebral vasodilation, increasing cerebral blood flow, and raises capillary pressure and permeability; fluid shifts into brain tissue, producing mild swelling in a rigid skull.
Fluid retention and a rise in sympathetic activity may contribute; the exact mechanism is not fully understood.
Risk falls with slow ascent that allows ventilatory acclimatisation to develop; descent reverses symptoms.
Severe forms include high altitude cerebral oedema and high altitude pulmonary oedema, which are medical emergencies.

blocks.title: Pressure, not percentage
blocks.text: Altitude lowers PIO2 because barometric pressure falls, not because oxygen makes up a smaller fraction of air. Everything else in the unit follows: the carotid bodies detect the fall in PaO2, hyperventilation partly compensates, the kidneys and marrow adapt over days to weeks, and AMS appears when ascent outpaces adaptation.

blocks.title: Teaching note on acetazolamide
blocks.text: Pharmacology teaching example only, not advice: acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, causes bicarbonate loss in the urine and a mild metabolic acidosis, and so accelerates the pH correction that drives ventilatory acclimatisation. It illustrates the physiology above rather than being a treatment instruction.

points: FIO2 stays at 0.21; PIO2 = 0.21 x (PB - 47) falls with barometric pressure, so alveolar and arterial PO2 fall.
Carotid body detection of hypoxia causes immediate hyperventilation; the resulting alkalosis limits it until renal bicarbonate excretion allows ventilation to rise further over days.
Erythropoietin from the kidney raises red cell mass over weeks, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity.
AMS arises from rapid ascent: hypoxia-induced cerebral vasodilation and fluid shift cause headache and related symptoms; slow ascent allows acclimatisation.

questions.stem: Why does alveolar PO2 fall at high altitude even though oxygen still makes up 21 percent of the air?

options.text: Barometric pressure is lower, so the partial pressure of oxygen is lower at the same fraction
The fraction of oxygen in air falls with altitude
Water vapour pressure in the airways falls with altitude
Carbon dioxide in the air increases with altitude

questions.correctOptionText: Barometric pressure is lower, so the partial pressure of oxygen is lower at the same fraction

distractorRationale.a: Correct: partial pressure equals fraction times total pressure, and total pressure falls with altitude.
distractorRationale.b: The oxygen fraction of dry air is constant at 0.21 at all altitudes reached by humans.
distractorRationale.c: Water vapour pressure is set by body temperature (47 mmHg at 37 degrees C) and is constant.
distractorRationale.d: Atmospheric carbon dioxide does not rise with altitude in a way that affects alveolar oxygen.

questions.explanation: By Dalton's law the partial pressure of a gas equals its fractional concentration times the total pressure. The fraction stays at 0.21 but PB falls, so PIO2 and therefore PAO2 fall. The driving pressure for oxygen diffusion is reduced even though the composition of the air is unchanged.

questions.stem: On the first day at 3,500 m, a trekker hyperventilates but ventilation increases less than the fall in PaO2 would predict. Which mechanism best explains this limitation?

options.text: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and raises CSF pH, reducing central chemoreceptor drive to breathe
Carotid bodies stop responding to hypoxia within hours
Hypoxia directly depresses the medullary respiratory neurons completely
Erythropoietin released by the kidney inhibits the respiratory centres

questions.correctOptionText: Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and raises CSF pH, reducing central chemoreceptor drive to breathe

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the respiratory alkalosis created by hyperventilation opposes further increase in ventilation until bicarbonate adjusts.
distractorRationale.b: Carotid body sensitivity actually increases with days at altitude.
distractorRationale.c: Hypoxia stimulates ventilation via the carotid bodies; severe hypoxia can depress neurons but that does not explain this finding.
distractorRationale.d: Erythropoietin acts on red cell precursors and has no role in respiratory drive.

questions.explanation: The carotid bodies stimulate ventilation, which lowers PaCO2 and raises plasma and CSF pH. The central chemoreceptors, which respond to H+ in brain extracellular fluid, then oppose the hypoxic stimulus. Only when renal and CSF bicarbonate fall over days is the brake released.

questions.stem: A mountaineer spending several weeks at altitude shows a rising haemoglobin concentration and red cell mass. Which sequence correctly describes the stimulus and mediator?

options.text: Renal hypoxia, increased erythropoietin from kidney interstitial cells, increased marrow red cell production
Pulmonary hypoxia, increased erythropoietin from the liver, increased spleen red cell destruction
Hypercapnia, increased renin release, increased marrow red cell production
Alkalosis, decreased erythropoietin, increased plasma volume

questions.correctOptionText: Renal hypoxia, increased erythropoietin from kidney interstitial cells, increased marrow red cell production

distractorRationale.a: Correct: low oxygen tension in the kidney stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor, raising erythropoietin that drives erythropoiesis.
distractorRationale.b: The adult kidney is the main source of erythropoietin, and splenic destruction would lower red cell mass.
distractorRationale.c: Altitude causes hypocapnia, not hypercapnia, and renin is not the stimulus for erythropoiesis.
distractorRationale.d: Erythropoietin increases, not decreases, in hypoxia, and plasma volume falls early at altitude.

questions.explanation: Reduced oxygen tension in the kidney stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor in peritubular interstitial cells, which raises erythropoietin secretion. Erythropoietin stimulates red cell precursors in the marrow, so red cell mass and oxygen-carrying capacity rise over weeks.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old flies to 3,500 m and develops a headache, nausea and poor sleep within 12 hours. Which pathophysiological process best explains the headache of acute mountain sickness?

options.text: Hypoxia-induced cerebral vasodilation with increased capillary pressure and fluid shift into brain tissue
Polycythaemia increasing blood viscosity and reducing cerebral flow
Hypercapnia from underventilation causing cerebral vasoconstriction
A fall in the oxygen fraction of inspired air to below 15 percent

questions.correctOptionText: Hypoxia-induced cerebral vasodilation with increased capillary pressure and fluid shift into brain tissue

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hypoxia dilates cerebral vessels, increasing flow and capillary pressure, and fluid shifts promote mild brain swelling.
distractorRationale.b: Polycythaemia takes weeks to develop and cannot explain symptoms within 12 hours.
distractorRationale.c: Altitude causes hyperventilation and hypocapnia, and hypercapnia would vasodilate, not constrict.
distractorRationale.d: The oxygen fraction does not change with altitude; the partial pressure falls.

questions.explanation: Acute mountain sickness follows ascent faster than acclimatisation. Hypoxia dilates cerebral vessels, raising blood flow and capillary pressure, and fluid shifts promote brain swelling in a rigid skull, which produces headache. The exact mechanism is not fully understood, but this is the accepted outline.

questions.stem: True or false: During ventilatory acclimatisation over several days, renal excretion of bicarbonate allows ventilation to rise further.
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation produces respiratory alkalosis, which restrains the central chemoreceptors. Renal bicarbonate excretion and a fall in CSF bicarbonate bring pH back towards normal, releasing this restraint so ventilation can increase further.

questions.stem: At a mountain pass the barometric pressure is 500 mmHg. Taking FIO2 as 0.21 and water vapour pressure as 47 mmHg, calculate the partial pressure of oxygen in humidified inspired air (PIO2) in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Subtract water vapour pressure from barometric pressure: 500 - 47 = 453 mmHg. Multiply by the oxygen fraction: 0.21 x 453 = 95.1 mmHg. Compared with about 150 mmHg at sea level, the oxygen fraction is unchanged but the partial pressure has fallen by roughly 37 percent.

questions.stem: At altitude a climber has PIO2 of 90 mmHg and, after hyperventilation, PaCO2 of 30 mmHg. Using the simplified alveolar gas equation with R = 0.8 and assuming alveolar PCO2 equals PaCO2, calculate alveolar PO2 in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Use PAO2 = PIO2 - PACO2 / R. PACO2 / R = 30 / 0.8 = 37.5 mmHg, so PAO2 = 90 - 37.5 = 52.5 mmHg. Without hyperventilation (PACO2 40) PAO2 would be 90 - 50 = 40 mmHg, so the lower PaCO2 gains the climber 12.5 mmHg of alveolar oxygen.

questions.stem: Explain why alveolar oxygen partial pressure falls at altitude despite an unchanged oxygen fraction, and how hyperventilation partly offsets this fall.
markingGuide: States FIO2 is constant at 0.21 but barometric pressure falls with altitude
Uses partial pressure = fraction x (PB - PH2O), with PH2O fixed at 47 mmHg, to show PIO2 falls
States alveolar PO2 follows inspired PO2 and the alveolar gas equation PAO2 = PIO2 - PACO2 / R
Explains hyperventilation lowers alveolar PCO2, so less oxygen is displaced and PAO2 rises
States hyperventilation is triggered by carotid body detection of low arterial PO2
questions.explanation: Dalton's law makes PIO2 equal to 0.21 x (PB - 47), so a fall in PB lowers PIO2 and thereby PAO2. The alveolar gas equation shows PAO2 = PIO2 - PACO2 / R, so ventilating more lowers PACO2 and restores some alveolar oxygen. The stimulus for hyperventilation is detection of low arterial PO2 by the carotid bodies.

questions.stem: Describe the ventilatory and haematological changes during the first days and weeks at altitude, stating the mechanism and time scale of each.
markingGuide: Immediate: carotid body detection of low PaO2 causes hyperventilation, lowering PaCO2 and producing respiratory alkalosis
Explains the initial rise is limited because alkalosis reduces central chemoreceptor drive
Over days: renal bicarbonate excretion and CSF pH correction release the brake, so ventilation rises further; carotid sensitivity increases
Hypoxia raises erythropoietin from the kidney, which stimulates the marrow
Red cell mass and oxygen-carrying capacity rise over weeks; early haemoglobin rise partly reflects reduced plasma volume
questions.explanation: The ventilatory response has two phases: a rapid but limited carotid body driven increase, followed by a further rise over days once renal bicarbonate excretion corrects the alkalosis. The haematological response is slower, with erythropoietin raising red cell mass over weeks. Early rises in haemoglobin concentration are partly due to loss of plasma volume.

questions.stem: Outline the pathophysiology of acute mountain sickness, explain why it follows rapid ascent, and say how slow ascent reduces the risk.
markingGuide: Hypoxia from reduced PIO2 causes cerebral vasodilation and increased cerebral blood flow
Increased capillary pressure and permeability lead to fluid shift and mild brain swelling in a rigid skull, producing headache
Notes fluid retention may contribute and that the full mechanism is incompletely understood
Rapid ascent outpaces ventilatory acclimatisation and renal bicarbonate compensation, so hypoxaemia is greater and lasts longer
Slow ascent allows the adaptive changes in ventilation to develop; descent reverses symptoms
questions.explanation: Hypoxia dilates cerebral vessels and raises capillary pressure, shifting fluid into brain tissue, which accounts for headache, nausea and other symptoms. Rapid ascent exposes the climber to low PaO2 before ventilatory acclimatisation can improve arterial oxygenation. Slow ascent gives time for these adaptations, so risk falls.
